examples: I thought I had sent the email, but it never arrived.
I was sure I had put my wallet in my bag, but when I went to buy something, it wasn't there.
I thought I understood this problem, but I got it wrong on the test.
I still thought of myself as young, so it was a shock when someone gave up their seat to me on the train.
I believed I was better at drawing than others, but when I went on to art college, there were lots of people who were far more talented.
I see her as just a friend, but she apparently wants to marry me. What a pain.
fields.explain:
Used for personal intentions; should not be imposed on the listener (avoid using it as a command).
To soften it: ～つもりだが／けど… (I intend to…, but…).
Vたつもり: nuance of self-justification/misunderstanding; often used with が/のに to state contrast.
Negative “～つもりはない”: strong, a firm refusal to do something.
Unnatural when asserting someone else's firm intention without a source: use ～つもりだそうだ／らしい.

• Personal intention/plan: the speaker intends to do / not to do something.
• Subjective/mistaken judgment: Vたつもりだ = thinking you did something when in fact you didn't, or it isn't so.
• Degree of certainty: stronger than “～と思う” in volition, weaker than “～予定だ” (a plan with a concrete schedule).
• With a third-person subject: usually the hearsay/conjecture form “～つもりらしい／～つもりだという” is used.
• Often followed by a contrasting clause: ～つもりだったのに (I meant to… but…).
fields.notes:
Note:
●主語が三人称（彼、彼女、田中さんなど）のときは使えない。
Cannot be used when the subject is third person (he, she, Mr. Tanaka, etc.).
1.  X彼は来年アメリカに留学するつもりです。
X He intends to study in the US next year.
2.  　→彼は来年アメリカに留学するつもりだと言っています。
→ He says he intends to study in the US next year.
Note:
●自分の意志で決められないことには使えない。
Cannot be used for things that cannot be decided by your own will.
1.  X　わたしは来年大学に合格するつもりです。
X I intend to pass the university entrance exam next year.
2.  X わたしは交通事故にあわないつもりです。
X I intend not to have a traffic accident.
mistakes: Using ～つもり for someone else's intention without a quotation or conjecture marker → unnatural or impolite.
Confusing ～つもりだ with ～予定だ: when the question calls for an official schedule, choose ～予定だ.
Mixing up V-たつもり (thought you had done it) with V-てしまった (ended up doing / did by accident) → different nuances.
Using つもり directly with an adjective → not used; switch to つもりで (adverbial) or another expression.

fields.meaning:
～するのが難しくてこまる
Doing ~ is difficult and troublesome
examples: It's a personal matter, so it's hard to ask people at work.
From this spot, it's hard to see what's written on the blackboard.

fields.meaning: Do and then go / continue onward
examples: to keep getting higher
Since the amount is decreasing worldwide, the price of oil will probably keep rising from now on.
If you keep living like this, you'll get fatter and fatter.
I intend to keep working hard so that I can get even better.
This writer will probably become famous from now on.
I intend to continue studying Japanese from now on.
fields.explain:
Direction “moving away”: in contrast with ～てくる (toward the speaker/the present).
When talking about strategies or visions: ～していく emphasizes continuity and initiative.
With a change of state: ～く/～に + なっていく is used for the future; ～なってきた is used for a change that has progressed up to the present.
The contracted spoken form ～てく is common, but should be avoided in formal written language.

• Spatial direction: the action moves away from the speaker/reference point (走っていく, 持っていく).
• Temporal direction: a process/degree of change will continue from now into the future (増えていく, 良くなっていく).
• Sequence of actions: do something and then go (食べていく can mean “eat and then go / go on”).
• Nuance of progression, long-term, long-range plans (この活動を続けていくつもりだ).
fields.notes:
• With verbs of motion, ～ていく can also mean “do something and then leave”: 食べていく, 見ていく.
• In narration, the past ～ていった/～ていった often describes moving away from the scene.
• Avoid using ～ていく for sudden, instantaneous events; it suits tendencies and progression better. | Meaning: moving away from the speaker (space) / change from now on (time)
mistakes: Confusing the direction with ～てくる: ×持ってくる when you are “taking it away”; it must be 持っていく.
Using ～ていく for past up to present: “has gradually … until now” requires ～てきた.
Confusing it with ～続ける: ～ていく has a future-oriented nuance, not just simple continuation.
Overusing the contraction ～てく in formal written language.

Preparing beforehand, does not show direction/future progression

fields.meaning: Wanting someone to do something | Want (someone) to do…
examples: I'd like you to be quiet, please.
I want you to come early tomorrow.
I want the children to read more books.
I hope he gets better.
I'd like you not to smoke here.
I would like you to check this matter by the end of today.
fields.explain:
Casual: Vてほしい／Vないでほしい。Polite: Vてほしいです。Very polite: Vていただきたいです。
Indirect, softer: ～てもらえるとありがたい／助かります。
When hoping for something natural (rain stopping), use が:雨 が やん でほしい。
Emphasizing strong emotion can sound demanding; consider the context.

• Expresses a desire/request for someone else to do an action (or for something to happen).
• The subject is usually the speaker (I/we). For a general desire: みんなに分かってほしい。
• Strength depends on the context: statement (hope), suggestion (request), complaint (don't do…).
• に marks “the person being asked”; が marks “the agent of the desired action/event”.
fields.notes:
• When speaking directly to the listener, add a polite opener: すみませんが／恐れ入りますが／できれば…＋Vていただきたい。
• “人に” vs “人が”: with a specific agent, both are possible; に emphasizes the person being asked, が emphasizes the event happening.
• In business writing, avoid commands: prefer 「ご対応いただけますと幸いです」。
mistakes: Using てほしい for a third party's desire → unnatural; to say “A wants B to do” you need たがっている/ほしがっている: 彼は私に来てほしがっている。
Confusing it with たい: “I want you to help” must be 手伝ってほしい, not 手伝いたい。
Leaving out に/が makes the agent ambiguous: “誰にしてほしいのか” needs to be clear.
JLPT: politeness trap – choose ていただきたい when addressing a superior/customer.

rows: Direct desire; the subject is the speaker.
The subject is the speaker; not used for others.
Want to have someone do it for you
More polite/tactful; emphasizes receiving a benefit.
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>してもらいたい。
Would like to have it done (keigo)
<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>していただきたいです。

examples: Please try pressing this button.
It looks spicy, but I'll try a little.
I tried the new app, and it's surprisingly handy.
Would you like to try it on to see if the size fits?
Let's try asking the teacher.
I bought a new magazine, so I tried reading it right away.
fields.explain:
Friendly; reduces the pressure of deciding (“just try it first”).
Often used as てみてください (please try), てみませんか (invitation), てみたい (desire).
Not used when the action is serious/high-risk (in that case use検討する/試みる...).

～てみる expresses “trying” an action to check the result/possibility/experience. みる here is an auxiliary verb meaning “try and see”, different from 見る “look”. The action is usually small-scale and exploratory, with no commitment to a result.
• Emphasizes experience: doing something to find out the result (アウトカム未知).
• Goes well with polite suggestions/recommendations in conversation.
• Distinguish from 試す/試みる: てみる is more casual/lighter; 試みる is very formal, written language.
fields.notes:
• てみる combines well with “trial” adverbs: とりあえず/まず/一度/少し.
• Negative: Vてみない (spoken) or Vてみません (polite negative, invitation form) means “why not try?”.
• When the goal is “checking whether something is possible”: ～かどうか + Vてみる is very natural. Example: 動くかどうか試しに動かしてみる。
mistakes: Attaching てみる to the potential form: ×食べられてみる → 〇食べてみる (てみる itself already carries the sense of trying).
Using てみる for actions that cannot be “tried”: ×死んでみる (unnatural/pragmatically inappropriate).
Confusing it with ようとする: てみる is trying (actually done), ようとする is “to intend, to be about to”.

rows: Emphasizes the intention at that point in time
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>しようとする
<ruby>新<rt>しん</rt></ruby><ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>試<rt>ため</rt></ruby>す

examples: I'm going to a party tomorrow, so I got my clothes out ahead of time.
Guests are coming, so I have to clean the room beforehand.
My friends are coming tomorrow, so I bought lots of drinks and food in advance.
“We'll read Lesson 3 next week, so please look up the meanings of the words beforehand.”
I'm thinking of getting my driver's license before I graduate.
“Please put the things you used back where they were.”
fields.explain:
Emphasizes “preparation” when there is a clear future purpose: 〜ために／〜に備えて + Vておく.
Request form: 〜しておいてください（please do it in advance / leave it as is）。
Contracted spoken forms are very common: しとく、買っとく、やっといて。
“Leave as is” often appears with そのままにしておく／開けておく／つけておく（leave on）.

Preparing in advance
1.
A:会議(かいぎ)の前(まえ)に　なにを しておきますか。
A: What should we prepare before the meeting?
B:資料(しりょう)を　コピーしておきます。
B: I'll make copies of the documents beforehand.
2.
A:旅行(りょこう)に行(い)く前(まえ)に何(なに)を　しておいたら　いいですか。
A: What should I do before going on a trip?
B: ホテルを予約(よやく)しておいたら　いいですよ。
B: You should book a hotel in advance.
Used to deal with a situation after doing an action, or to offer a temporary solution.
1.
A: この本(ほん)は　どう　しましょうか。
A: What should I do with this book?
B:読(よ)んだら、本棚(ほんだな)に戻(もど)しておいてください。
B: When you've finished reading it, please put it back on the bookshelf.
2.
A: ナイフと　フォークは　どこに　しまいましょうか。
A: Where should I put away the knives and forks?
B:元(もと)の所(ところ)に　しまっておいてください。
B: Please put them back where they were.
Keeping or maintaining a certain state.
1.
A:片付(かたづ)けましょうか。
A: Shall I tidy up?
B: もうすぐ会社(かいしゃ)に行(い)く時間(じかん)ですから、そのままに　しておいてください。
B: It's almost time to go to work, so please just leave it as it is.
2.
A:窓(まど)を　しめてもいいですか。
A: May I close the window?
B: すみません、ちょっと　あついですから、そのまま　あけておいてください。
B: Sorry, it's a bit hot, so please leave it open.
We can conjugate the verb おく into the appropriate forms.
fields.notes:
• With devices/electricity: つけておく（turn on in advance）、消しておく（turn off in advance）、充電しておく（charge in advance） are very natural.
• The negative ないでおく has a deliberate nuance of “leaving it for later”: 今は触らないでおく。
• In business email: あらかじめ共有しておきます（I am sharing this in advance） is a polite set phrase.
meaning_vi: Expresses doing something so that there are no difficulties later, or so that something is thoroughly prepared. As in example ④, this sentence pattern is sometimes also used to mean keeping a state as it is. Usually used with verbs expressing volitional actions.
examples: 1. ①荷物をかばんに入れておきます。
I'll put my things in the bag in advance.
2. ②ごみを外に出しておきましょう。
Let's take the trash outside beforehand.
3. ③旅行の話はサラに伝えておいたよ。
I already told Sarah about the trip.
4. ④窓はそのまま開けておいてください。
Please leave the window open as it is.
The structure「Nを～ておく」expresses an action prepared in advance for the future. The structure「Nが～てある」expresses the result of an action.
1. ①　書いておく／書いてある
Write in advance / Is written
2. ②　他の人のかさと間違えないように、ここに名前を書いておこう／買いとこう。
Let's write our names here so we don't mix up our umbrellas with other people's.
3. ③　明日から国に帰るので、お土産を買っておいた。
I'm going back to my country tomorrow, so I bought souvenirs in advance.
4. ➃　これはだれのかさだろう？あっ、ここに名前が書いてある。
Whose umbrella is this? Oh, there's a name written here.
mistakes: Confusing it with 〜てある: “already there” (結果状態) uses てある; “do in advance” (intentional, future-oriented action) uses ておく. The JLPT often sets traps: ドアが（開けてある／開けておく）.
Using ておく for actions with no sense of “preparation” sounds forced.
Forgetting the “leave as is” nuance: 片付けないでおく（deliberately not tidying up) differs from 片付けていない（simply the state of not having tidied up).

Existing result; does not emphasize “the future”

fields.meaning: Do and come back / gradually become…
examples: My friend called me again.
This is food from my home country that my mother sent me.
I'm just going to pop out and buy a drink at the convenience store.
I'll go print out the documents and be right back, so please wait a moment.
It suddenly started raining.
Prices have gone up lately.
fields.explain:
Common in spoken language:行ってくる (I'm going out for a bit and will be back), いってきます (set phrase when leaving home).
Emphasizes the result “has arrived / up to the present”: ～てきた is often used with verbs of change:増える／減る／慣れる／分かる／見えてくる.
Compared with ～ていく:寒くなって きた : it has started getting cold up to now.これからもっと寒くなって いく : it will get colder from now on.
寒くなって きた : it has started getting cold up to now.
これからもっと寒くなって いく : it will get colder from now on.
Used with verbs of motion/bringing:持ってくる,連れてくる,呼んでくる.

• It is not just “come”, but “an event/action/change happens and its result is present with the speaker or at the present time”.
• Two major groups of meaning:

Spatial meaning: 行ってくる, 買ってくる, 持ってくる (go do something / bring it here).
Temporal/abstract meaning: ～てきた (has gradually), ～ていく (will gradually from now on). くる points toward the present, いく toward the future/moving away.

• Spatial meaning: 行ってくる, 買ってくる, 持ってくる (go do something / bring it here).
• Temporal/abstract meaning: ～てきた (has gradually), ～ていく (will gradually from now on). くる points toward the present, いく toward the future/moving away.
• The form てきている emphasizes a state that has begun and continues up to the present.
fields.notes:
• With emotions/perception: 実感してきた, 見えてきた (has gradually become clear).
• Causative form + くる in spoken language: 待たせてきてごめん (went to do X before coming, making you wait).
• 電話してくる contains the meaning “call (toward me)”; 電話していく is rare and has a different meaning.
meaning_vi: Expresses a change of state that has occurred up to the present or up to a certain point in time.
V:　太って　+　くる
explain: Expresses emotions, states, or natural phenomena that arise or increase gradually over time. Emphasizes the process of “gradually appearing”.
examples: 1. 健康に関心を持つ人が増えてきました。
More and more people have become interested in their health.
2. ４月に入って、だんだん暖かくなってきました。
Now that it's April, it has been getting gradually warmer.
──────
1. 悲しくて、涙が出てきた。
I was so sad that tears started to come.
2. こう暑いと、じっとしていても汗が出てくる。
When it's this hot, you start sweating even if you stay still.
3. そのときはあまり感じなかったが、あとになって怒りがわいてきた。
I didn't feel much at the time, but later anger welled up in me.
4. しばらくしてから、優勝の喜びがこみあげてきた。
After a while, the joy of winning welled up.
──────
1. ①　痛くなってきた
It has started to hurt
2. ②　石油の値段がだんだん高くなってきた。
The price of oil has gradually gone up.
3. ③　運動しなかったので、だんだん太ってきた。
I didn't exercise, so I gradually gained weight. | Meaning: toward the speaker (space) / change from the past up to now (time)
mistakes: Mixing up てくる and ていく in temporal direction: ✕ これから寒くなってきます (hasn't happened yet) → ✓ なっていきます.
Using てくる with verbs that have no sense of progression makes it hard to understand: ✕ 知ってきた → usually 分かってきた/理解できるようになってきた.
Confusing “bring here” vs “take away”: ここに持っていって is the wrong direction; it must be 持ってきて.
The JLPT often tests the contrast: 降ってきた (started raining) vs 降っている (is raining) vs 降っていく (rarely used).

<ruby>気温<rt>きおん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がっていく

fields.connection: Vても / Aくても / N・Naでも + [sentence/clause]
examples: 「If I take a taxi now, will I make it in time?」
「Is it impossible to do this job without experience?」
「Tomorrow is my birthday. Even if you're busy, be sure to come, okay?」
「No matter how much you dislike them, you should eat vegetables for your health.」
For various reasons, there are many children who can't study even though they want to.
「Mr. Hayashi's grandfather is still so healthy no matter how old he gets. That's wonderful.」
fields.explain:
Emphasizes that something “has no effect / does not change the decision”.
Often used with emphatic words: たとえ／いくら／どんなに／もし.
Can be used with commands/advice, but is more natural when stating a position:雨でも来てください（acceptable), though the style is a bit stiff.

• Concession/concessive condition: “even if … still …”; the result is not affected by the condition in the first clause.
• Used for suppositions or for real, repeated situations.
• With a question word＋でも/ても it means “no matter how … / regardless of …”: 何をしても, いつでも.
fields.notes:
• N/Na＋でも, Aい→Aくても, Vて＋も: be careful to change each word type correctly.
• Negative: Aくなくても, Na/N＋じゃなくても, Vなくても.
• Fixed emphatic phrases: たとえ～ても／いくら～ても／どんなに～ても.
mistakes: Wrong conjugation: ×高いでも → correct: 高くても; ×静かくても → correct: 静かでも.
Confusing it with ～のに (a fact contrary to expectation). ～ても can be a supposition; ～のに is a fact.
Using ～てもいい instead of ～ても when you mean “even if … still …” → wrong meaning.
Mistaken “雨でても” (wrong connection) → correct: 雨でも.

rows: A fact contrary to expectation; nuance of dissatisfaction.
<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるとしても<ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>る。
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>くたって<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>わない。
